title: Beyond Geometry: Hole-Edge Atomic Configuration as a Design Variable in Graphyne Kirigami
authors: Guilherme B. Kanegae, Alexandre F. Fonseca
abstract: Kirigami-inspired cuts are an established route to stretchability in two-dimensional materials. At the nanoscale, however, cut edges are not purely geometric: they comprise discrete atomic configurations that can alter the mechanical response. In graphene, a given cut geometry fixes the edge structure; graphyne, a porous carbon allotrope with an intrinsic band gap, lifts this constraint, as identical cut geometries can yield distinct hole-edge configurations. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we report the first atomistic study of $γ$-graphyne kirigami (GYK), and compared with graphene kirigami. GYK reaches yield strains up to 9.6 times that of pristine $γ$-graphyne, with a response governed by both cut geometry and local hole-edge structure. Removing just two carbon atoms at selected edge sites further raises the yield strain by up to 35%, with little loss of yield stress. These findings identify hole-edge atomic configuration as an additional design parameter, expanding the design space for nanoscale kirigami engineering.
summary: This work investigates graphyne kirigami, a material where mechanical stretchability is enhanced by patterned cuts. The authors demonstrate that the atomic arrangement at the cut edges, previously ignored, acts as a crucial, independent design variable. By tuning this hole-edge configuration, they significantly enhance the material's yield strength and overall mechanical performance.
main_problem: To expand the design space for nanoscale kirigami engineering by identifying the hole-edge atomic configuration as an additional design variable beyond just cut geometry.
main_result: The mechanical response of graphyne kirigami is governed by both cut geometry and the local hole-edge atomic structure, with edge modification significantly boosting yield strain.
method: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations were used to model the mechanical response of graphyne kirigami structures under tensile loading.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Graphyne Kirigami (GYK), a porous carbon allotrope, comparing its mechanical behavior to graphene kirigami (GRK). The structure's mechanical properties depend on the cut geometry and the specific atomic arrangement at the cut edges (hole-edge configuration).
key_observables: Yield strain ($\epsilon_{	ext{yield}}$), yield stress ($\sigma_{	ext{yield}}$), and effective elastic moduli ($E_1, E_2$).
important_parameters: Cut geometry parameters ($\alpha,  eta$), and the choice of hole-edge atomic configuration (e.g., acetylenic vs. benzene ring).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the mechanical response can be characterized by distinct deformation stages (flipping, stretching, fracture) and that the effective stiffness can be modeled by fitting the second deformation regime.
figures_summary: Figures show stress-strain curves, the evolution of bond counts/displacements during deformation, and the dependence of yield strain and effective moduli on geometric parameters ($\alpha$ and $ eta$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical system and the new design variable (hole-edge configuration). It then uses MD simulations to characterize the mechanical response, analyzing the dependence of yield strain and effective moduli on geometric ratios ($\alpha,  eta$) and the specific edge structure.
why_interesting: While the core physics is condensed matter mechanics, the systematic identification of atomic-scale structural variations (hole-edge configuration) as a quantifiable, tunable design parameter is analogous to engineering control over quantum boundary conditions or material interfaces in quantum devices.

Atoms highlighted in blue were displaced rigidly during simulations. (b, c) Atomic configurations at the hole edges, terminated by (b) an acetylenic linkage or (c) a benzene ring.

Figure 3: (a) Stress-strain curves of GYK12 structures with varying number of unit cells. (b) Yield strain (εyield) as a function of the number of unit cells. The inset shows representative snapshots of the 3-, 5-, and 7-cell structures.

Figure 4: (a, b) Yield strain (εyield) and (c, d) yield stress (σyield) as a function of α (left) and β (right). Results are normalized by the corresponding value of its pristine counterparts: γ-GY for the GYK structures (squares, triangles, and circles) and graphene for the GRK (stars). The yellow background indicates the region α < 0, where internal and edge cuts do not overlap and the structure behaves as a cut-free nanoribbon without the deformation mechanism illustrated in Figure 2b. Dashed lines are guides to the eye. In all panels the error bars are smaller than the symbol size (≲0.1 in (a, b) and ≲0.002 in (c, d), see Section S5).

Figure 5: Effective moduli of the (a, b) first, E1, and (c, d) second, E2, deformation stages as a function of α (left) and β (right). E1 was obtained from a linear fit through the origin over the entire first deformation stage and E2 from a linear fit to the region immediately preceding εyield (see Section S3). Error bars correspond to the standard deviation of the fitted slopes. Dashed lines in (a) and (c) are guides to the eye. Solid lines in (b) and (d) are least-squares fits of E = C1 exp(C2 · β) + C3 to each structure type.
